Widow of Zarephath
WID-oh uv ZAR-eh-fath
noun phrase (a Gentile widow)
From Zarephath (Hebrew Tsarephath, “smelting place”), a town of Zidon; the Greek of Luke renders it Sarepta. The widow whom God commanded to sustain Elijah in the famine.

📖 Biblical Definition

The widow of Zarephath was a Gentile woman of Zidon whom the LORD appointed to sustain Elijah during the three-year famine of Ahab's reign. When the brook Cherith dried up, God sent His prophet not to a daughter of Israel but to a heathen city, that mercy might be shown beyond the covenant nation. Elijah found her at the gate gathering two sticks, with but a handful of meal in a barrel and a little oil in a cruse, preparing a last meal for herself and her son that they might eat it and die. The prophet bade her fear not, and make him a little cake first, upon the word of the LORD that the barrel of meal should not waste nor the cruse of oil fail until rain returned to the earth. She believed and obeyed, putting the man of God's word before her own famished child, and the meal and oil failed not many days. When afterward her son fell sick and died, Elijah stretched himself upon the child and cried unto the LORD, and the soul of the child came into him again—the first raising of the dead recorded in Scripture. Our Lord Himself appealed to her in the synagogue at Nazareth, that Elias was sent to none of the widows of Israel save unto a woman of Sidon, to rebuke the unbelief of His own and to declare that the mercy of God overleaps the bounds of natural Israel. She is the dictionary's early type of Gentile inclusion: a heathen widow who lived by faith in the bare word of God and saw the dead raised.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Gentile widow of Sidon who fed Elijah from her failing barrel of meal at the word of the LORD, saw the meal and oil unfailing, and received her dead son raised; a type of Gentile inclusion cited by Christ at Nazareth.

expand to see more

WIDOW OF ZAREPHATH, noun phrase. A Gentile widow of Zarephath in Sidon, divinely appointed to sustain the prophet Elijah in the famine.

She had but a handful of meal and a little oil, and was preparing a last meal for herself and her son.

At Elijah's word she fed the prophet first, and the meal and oil failed not until the rain returned.

Her son died and was raised when Elijah stretched himself upon him and cried unto the LORD.

Christ named her at Nazareth (Luke 4:26) as a sign that God's mercy reaches beyond natural Israel to the Gentiles.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Ki 17:9 — "Arise, get thee to Zarephath, which belongeth to Zidon, and dwell there: behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee."

1 Ki 17:12 — "And she said, As the LORD thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die."

1 Ki 17:16 — "And the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Elijah."

Lu 4:26 — "But unto none of them was Elias sent, save unto Sarepta, a city of Sidon, unto a woman that was a widow."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is to make her merely a tale of charity or of feminine resilience, missing the faith in the bare word of God and the Gentile mercy her story announces.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is justifying faith resting on nothing but the promise of God. The widow had a single meal between her household and starvation, yet at Elijah's word she gave the prophet's portion first. This is not reckless generosity but the obedience of faith: she staked her last bread on the word of the LORD that the barrel should not waste, and the LORD honoured His word. To read her as a lesson in human kindness or in womanly grit is to lose the gospel in her story.

Her account also rebukes the parochialism that would confine the mercy of God to the natural seed. Our Lord pressed this very point in the synagogue at Nazareth and was nearly thrown from a cliff for it: that Elias passed over many widows in Israel and was sent to a Gentile of Sidon. So God prepared, centuries before, a witness that the gospel would go to the nations, and that a heathen widow living by faith would shame the unbelief of the covenant people. She belongs with Rahab and Ruth among the foretokens of Gentile inclusion.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Zarephath (Hebrew Tsarephath, “a place of smelting or refining”), a town of Zidon; the famine sets the refining of her faith over the refining furnace her town was named for.

expand to see more

Tsarephath, Hebrew, “smelting place” or “refinery,” a town of the Sidonian coast.

Sarepta, the Greek form of the name as quoted by Luke 4:26.

Almanah, Hebrew, a widow, one of the classes of the helpless God commands His people to defend.

The “barrel” (Hebrew kad) and “cruse” (tsappachath) are the humble vessels through which God multiplied bread.

Elijah's raising of her son is the first resurrection from the dead recorded in the canon.

Usage

"The pastor preached the widow of Zarephath to teach that faith gives God the first portion and trusts His bare word for the rest."

"He reminded the congregation that Christ Himself named her to prove that the mercy of God reaches the Gentiles."

"She found in the unfailing barrel of meal a parable of the daily bread that never fails the household of faith."
